segments.translit: ghanānandotkīrṇatayā kṛṣṇācāryapādāś cittagajendraśabdasandhyābhāṣayā tam evārtham utprekṣayanta āhuḥ |
segments.translation: Because he is suffused with dense [joy]{ananda}, the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the words 'the [mind]{citta}, a lord of [elephants]{elephant}', speaks, casting that same meaning as a [poetic fancy]{utpreksa}.
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song (cp.09.m1): [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, suffused with dense joy, speaks in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, using the words 'the mind, a lord of elephants', and casts that same meaning as a [poetic fancy]{utpreksa}. For Munidatta, then, the elephant of the song is the mind.

equations.en: the mind, as a lord of elephants

flags.note: ghanānandotkīrṇatayā: utkīrṇa is literally 'carved, engraved', and also 'filled, overflowing'. I render 'suffused with dense joy'; the literal alternative is 'engraved with dense joy'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dga' ba'i tshogs pas khyab pa, 'pervaded by a mass of joy', taking ghana as 'mass' and utkīrṇa as 'pervaded'.
tam evārtham, 'that same meaning': probably the meaning of the songs before this one, now put in a new figure; it could also point ahead to what the song goes on to say. Kept literal.

Shastri prints cittagajendraśavda sandhyābhāṣayā as two words. I read one compound, cittagajendraśabdasandhyābhāṣayā, 'in the twilight language of the word mind-lord-of-elephants'; the Tibetan sems kyi glang po che'i dgongs pa'i skad kyis takes it the same way.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ends de nyid kyi don gyi gzugs kyi rgyun du gsungs, 'spoke in a stream of form of that very meaning'. rgyun is probably a slip for rgyan: gzugs kyi rgyan, 'ornament of form', is how it renders utprekṣā elsewhere (cp.08.m2). It calls the poet nag po glu dbyangs zhabs for Kṛṣṇācāryapāda.

segments.translit:
evaṃkāra ityādi | ekāraś candrābhāsaṃ vaṃkāraḥ sūryaḥ ubhayaṃ divārātrijñānaṃ vākhoṛa stambhadvayaṃ mardayitvā nirābhāsīkṛtya vajrajāpakrameṇa | aparaṃ vividhaprakārān avadhūtīvyāpakabandhana[ṃ] toṛia toṛayitvā eṣāṃ trayāṇām anupalambhāsavapānena pramatta[ḥ] san jñānagajendrakṛṣṇācāryacaraṇāḥ | nalinīvanaṃ mahāsukhakamalaṃ kṛtvā nirvikalpākāre krīḍantīti |
tathācāryanāgārjunapādāḥ —
bāhyaṃ yat tad asat svabhāvavirahāj jñānañ ca vīkṣya cyavat
śūnyaṃ yat parikalpitaṃ tad api cāśūnyaṃ mataṃ kevalam |
ity evaṃ paribhāvya bhāvavibhavaṃ nirvinnatattvaikadhīr
māyānāṭaka[nāṭa]naikanipuṇo yogīśvaraḥ krīḍati ||
segments.translation:
'[Evaṃkāra]{evamkara}…' and so on. The syllable e is the [moon]{moon}-[appearance]{abhasa}, the syllable vaṃ the [sun]{surya}; the two together are the knowledge of day and night. The [post]{bakhora} (vākhoṛa) is the pair of pillars. Having crushed them and made them free of [appearance]{abhasa} through the process of [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}; further, having broken (toṛia) the [bonds]{bandhana} of many kinds that pervade the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}; and being intoxicated by drinking the [liquor]{asava} of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of these three, the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, the lord of [elephants]{elephant} who is knowledge, makes the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} the [lotus]{lotus} of [great bliss]{mahasukha} and plays in a form free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}.
So the master, the venerable [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna}, says:
What is external is unreal, since it lacks a [nature]{svabhava} of its own; and knowledge, when examined, slips away;
whatever is imagined as empty, that too is held to be simply not empty.
Having contemplated the display of things in this way, disenchanted, his mind one-pointed on [reality]{tattva},
the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, uniquely skilled in performing the drama of [illusion]{maya}, plays.
segments.note: Munidatta makes e the moon-appearance and vaṃ the sun, and the [post]{bakhora} a pair of pillars, apparently that same pair, crushed by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}; the bonds pervade the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the central channel. Drunk on the liquor of [non-apprehension]{anupalambha}, Kṛṣṇācārya makes the lotus grove the lotus of great bliss and plays free of concepts (cp.09.m2). The Tibetan reverses e and vaṃ.

equations.en: the knowledge of day and night
the lotus of great bliss, into which Kṛṣṇācārya makes the lotus grove

citations.quoted: bāhyaṃ yat tad asat svabhāvavirahāj jñānañ ca vīkṣya cyavat / śūnyaṃ yat parikalpitaṃ tad api cāśūnyaṃ mataṃ kevalam / ity evaṃ paribhāvya bhāvavibhavaṃ nirvinnatattvaikadhīr / māyānāṭaka[nāṭa]naikanipuṇo yogīśvaraḥ krīḍati
citations.work: No work named. Munidatta attributes the verse to the master Nāgārjuna (the Tibetan has 'phags pa klu sgrub, 'the noble Nāgārjuna'). I cannot identify the source.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reverses the syllables: baM yig zla ba'i snang ba e yig nyi ma, 'the syllable vaṃ is the moon-appearance, the syllable e the sun'. It also has nyin mo dang mtshan mo'i shes rab, 'the wisdom (prajñā) of day and night', for divārātrijñāna. I follow the Sanskrit (e = moon, vaṃ = sun), as the glossary's evamkara entry does.

The gerunds (mardayitvā, nirābhāsīkṛtya, toṛayitvā, kṛtvā) all depend on krīḍanti at the end; Shastri's daṇḍas break one sentence into three. I take vākhoṛa stambhadvayaṃ as the song's word with its Sanskrit rendering, in apposition to ubhayam, so that the pair of pillars is e and vaṃ themselves. This is looser than a stated equation; the bakhora entry is more cautious. Munidatta's pillars are two (dual), the Tibetan ka gnyis likewise, where the draft of 1a has one post.

vividhaprakārān (accusative plural masculine) does not agree with bandhana[ṃ] (neuter singular; Shastri restores the anusvāra). vyāpakabandhana toṛia seems to echo the song's biāpaka bāndhaṇa toṛiu, so the case may be loose. I translate plural 'bonds', with the draft. I take aparam as adverbial, 'further'; the Tibetan gzhan, 'other', reads it as 'the other' binding, a second thing besides the pillars.

For the bonds the Tibetan has rdo rje bzlas pas gzhan sna tshogs pa'i rab tu byed pa a wa d+hU tI khyab byed 'gog pa phyung nas, 'by vajra recitation, having pulled out the other, many-kinded, the obstruction pervading the avadhūtī': 'gog pa, 'obstruction', for bandhana, phyung, 'pulled out', for toṛayitvā. It also attaches vajra recitation to this clause, not to the crushing of the pillars.
eṣāṃ trayāṇām, 'of these three': not named. Perhaps the moon-appearance, the sun and the bonds, or the two pillars and the bonds; the Tibetan gsum po de rnams is equally vague. Translated literally.

The Tibetan has yod pa'i shes pa la glang po che'i dbang por spyod pa'i zhabs kyis gsungs so, 'the venerable one who acts as lord of elephants in the knowledge of what exists said this'. It seems to read san jñāna° as sajjñāna, 'knowledge of the existent', drops Kṛṣṇa, renders ācārya as spyod pa, and adds a verb 'said'. The Sanskrit is clear: pramattaḥ san, 'being intoxicated', then jñānagajendra, 'lord of elephants who is knowledge'.

The Tibetan has bde ba chen po'i chu skyes kyi tshal du phyin na, 'having gone to the lotus grove of great bliss', where the Sanskrit has nalinīvanaṃ mahāsukhakamalaṃ kṛtvā, 'having made the lotus grove the lotus of great bliss', as if reading gatvā for kṛtvā.

nirvikalpākāre krīḍanti, 'plays in a form free of conceptual thought', stands where the refrain has bilasaa ('plays') and nibitā ('at peace'); it may paraphrase both. It is not an explicit gloss of nibitā. The Tibetan song has sems med gyur, 'became mindless'.

Verse, line 1: jñānañ ca vīkṣya cyavat barely construes, and cyavat (an active participle of cyu, normally middle) is irregular. I translate as printed, 'knowledge, when examined, slips away'. The Tibetan shes pa yang ni phyi rol don bzhin no, 'knowledge too is like the external object', points to jñānañ ca bāhyārthavat. That reading scans (the verse is in śārdūlavikrīḍita, and every other line scans as printed), and in Bengali script বাহ্যার্থবৎ could be misread as বীক্ষ্য চ্যবৎ. If adopted: 'and knowledge is like the external object'.

Verse, line 2: I divide cāśūnyaṃ as ca aśūnyam: an emptiness that is imagined is itself 'not empty'. kevalam might instead go with the subject ('that alone'). The Tibetan de yang stong nyid 'dod pa 'ba' zhig min, 'that too is not held to be emptiness alone', is close in sense.

Verse, line 3: bhāvavibhava may be 'the display (or abundance) of things', as the Tibetan dngos tshogs, 'mass of things', takes it, or 'being and its cessation' (vibhava in its Buddhist sense). nirvinna is probably nirviṇṇa, 'disenchanted'; the Tibetan de nyid med la de nyid gcig pa'i blos seems to read a negative with tattva ('in the absence of reality') and then tattvaikadhī.

Verse, line 4: Shastri's restoration [nāṭa] (māyānāṭakanāṭanaikanipuṇo) is confirmed by the metre and by the Tibetan sgyu ma'i gar mkhan gar gyi bya ba la, 'in the dance-acts of the dancer of illusion'.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇa tam evam āhuḥ | jima jimetyādi |
yathā bāhyakarī kariṇyām īrṣyāmadaṃ vahati | tadvad bhagavatīnairātmāsaṅgatayā cittagajendrakṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ tathatāmadaṃ pravarṣanti |
segments.translation: With the next [verse]{pada} he says the same thing in this way. 'The more…' and so on. Just as an outer [elephant]{elephant} carries the [ichor]{mada} of jealousy toward a [she-elephant]{karini}, so the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, the lord of [elephants]{elephant} who is the [mind]{citta}, through his attachment to the [Blessed Lady]{p-bhagavati} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, rains down the [ichor]{mada} of [suchness]{tathata}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as a simile (cp.09.m3): as an outer elephant carries the [ichor]{mada} of jealousy toward a she-elephant, so Kṛṣṇācārya, the mind as lord of elephants, through attachment to the Blessed Lady [Nairātmā]{nairatma} (selflessness as a goddess), rains down the ichor of suchness. The she-elephant answers to Nairātmā only through the simile.

equations.en: Kṛṣṇācārya himself, the mind as lord of elephants

flags.note: bhagavatīnairātmāsaṅgatayā divides either as -āsaṅgatayā, 'through attachment (āsaṅga) to', or as -saṅgatayā, 'through union with'. I chose attachment: āsaṅga + -tā is a regular abstract where saṅgatā is not, the simile turns on the elephant's desire, cp.09.m5 uses anāsaṅga, 'non-attachment', and the Tibetan has bdag med ma la chags pa, 'attachment to Nairātmā'. The glossary entries karini, mada and p-bhagavati currently say 'union'.

īrṣyāmada: īrṣyā is 'jealousy, envy'; a bull elephant in rut is proverbially jealous and combative. I render 'the ichor of jealousy'. The mada entry paraphrases 'ichor of passion', and the Tibetan has chags pa'i myos pa, 'the intoxication of desire'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has phyi rol du glang po che glang mo la chags pa'i myos pas rgyug par byed, 'outwardly an elephant runs with the intoxication of desire for a she-elephant' (rgyug, 'run', for vahati, 'carries'). In the second half it spells out sems ni glang po che'i dbang po, 'the mind is the lord of elephants', and has de bzhin nyid kyi chang, 'the liquor of suchness', for tathatāmada.

segments.translit:
ataeva tṛtīyapadena bhāvānāṃ svarūpopalabdhim āhuḥ |
chaṛigai ityādi | aṇḍajā jarāyujā upapādukā[ḥ] saṃsvedajā devāsurādiprakṛtikāḥ | sarve bhāvāḥ svabhāvena pariśuddhā yogīndrasya | bālāgram apy apariśuddhaṃ kiñcin na vidyate |
tathā ca madhyamakaśāstraḥ —
nāpaneyam ataḥ kiñcit prakṣeptavyaṃ na kiñcana |
draṣṭavyaṃ bhūtato bhūtaṃ bhūtadarśī vimucyate ||
segments.translation:
Therefore, with the third [verse]{pada}, he speaks of the apprehension of the [true nature]{svarupa} of things. 'The [six realms]{sadgati}…' and so on. Those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born spontaneously and those born from moisture, whose nature is that of gods, asuras and the rest: for the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, all things are pure by [nature]{svabhava}. Nothing impure exists, not even the tip of a hair.
And so the [Madhyamakaśāstra]{tx-madhyamakasastra} says:
Nothing is to be removed from this, nothing whatever to be added.
The real is to be seen as real; one who sees the real is freed.
segments.note: Munidatta says this couplet speaks of apprehending the [true nature]{svarupa} of things (cp.09.m4): all beings, however born, gods, asuras or others, are pure by nature for the lord of yogis, without a hair's tip of impurity. A Madhyamaka verse follows: nothing to remove or add; whoever sees the real is freed. The Tibetan reads 'things and non-things'.

equations.en: beings born from eggs, wombs, moisture or spontaneously, of the nature of gods, asuras and the rest

citations.quoted: nāpaneyam ataḥ kiñcit prakṣeptavyaṃ na kiñcana | draṣṭavyaṃ bhūtato bhūtaṃ bhūtadarśī vimucyate ||
citations.work: Madhyamakaśāstra, as Munidatta names it. The verse is a well-known one, found with small variants in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra (5.21) and the Ratnagotravibhāga (1.154), neither of them a Madhyamaka treatise by title; which work he means is unclear. Verse numbers are from memory.

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit has bhāvānāṃ svarūpopalabdhi, 'the apprehension of the true nature of things', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dngos po dang dngos po med pa'i dmigs pa, 'the apprehension of things and non-things', echoing bhābābhāba of line 4b, which the Sanskrit comment does not repeat.

upalabdhi, 'apprehension, perception', comes from the same root as the anupalambha, 'non-apprehension', of cp.09.m2. Here it is the true nature that is apprehended; Munidatta does not comment on the contrast. 'Realization' would also do.

The Tibetan lists the births in the usual order (egg, womb, moisture, spontaneous) and attaches 'gods, asuras and the rest' to the spontaneously born (rdzus te skyes pa'i lha dang lha ma yin); the Sanskrit puts upapāduka third and saṃsvedaja fourth, with devāsurādiprakṛtikāḥ qualifying the whole list.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena paripakvakuśalalakṣaṇam āhuḥ —
daśabaletyādi daśabalavaiśāradyādiguṇayuktaṃ tathatāratnaṃ daśadigvyāpakatayā anubhavābhyāsabalena hāritam asmākaṃ | ataeva tathatāratnaprabhāveṇāvidyākarīndrasyānāsaṅgena(ṇa) damanaṃ (madanaṃ) kuru || 9 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of the mark of ripened [virtue]{kusala}. 'The [ten powers]{dasabala}…' and so on. The [jewel]{ratna} of [suchness]{tathata}, endowed with the qualities of the [ten powers]{dasabala}, the [fearlessnesses]{vaisaradya} and the rest, has been taken by us, as pervading the [ten directions]{dasadis}, through the strength of habituation to direct experience. Therefore, by the power of the [jewel]{ratna} of [suchness]{tathata}, tame, through non-attachment, the lord of [elephants]{elephant} that is [ignorance]{avidya}.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet the mark of ripened [virtue]{kusala} (cp.09.m5): the jewel of suchness, with the ten powers and fearlessnesses, pervading the ten directions, is 'taken by us' through habituation to experience; by its power one is to tame, without attachment, the elephant of ignorance (the song has knowledge). The Tibetan has the jewel radiating, and intoxication for taming.

equations.en: the jewel of suchness, endowed with the ten powers, the fearlessnesses and other qualities
the lord of elephants that is ignorance

flags.note: damanaṃ (madanaṃ): Shastri prints damanaṃ, 'taming', with madanaṃ, 'intoxicating', in parentheses. Which is the manuscript and which his correction is not clear from the pack. damanaṃ matches the song's damakum̐; the Tibetan ma chags pa'i myos pa, 'intoxication without attachment', supports madanaṃ. I translate damanaṃ. With madanaṃ the sentence would say, roughly, 'make the lord of elephants that is ignorance intoxicated, without attachment'.

Munidatta has ignorance where the song has knowledge: the sandhi prabhāveṇāvidyā° requires avidyā, and the Tibetan comment agrees (ma rig pa'i glang po che'i dbang po), though the Tibetan song has rig pa'i glang dbang. He puts anāsaṅgena, 'through non-attachment', where the song has akilesem̐, 'without affliction', and makes the verb an imperative (kuru, addressed to no one named) where the draft of 5b has 'I tame'. Shastri's (ṇa) after anāsaṅgena is an orthographic variant that does not change the sense.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nyams su myong ba goms pa'i stobs kyis 'phro ba, 'radiates through the strength of habituation to experience', for hāritam, 'taken', as its version of the song line has phyogs bcu rnams su 'phro, 'radiates into the ten directions'. Its dag nyid kyi'o is perhaps a slip for bdag nyid kyi'o, 'our own', rendering asmākam. It ends gang las so, 'from which', and has no imperative.

hāritam is formally a causative participle ('caused to be taken'; in other contexts also 'carried off, lost'). With asmākam I take it as 'has been taken by us', echoing the song's haria, 'seizing'. The Tibetan has dge ba'i rtsa ba yongs su smin pa, 'fully ripened roots of virtue', for paripakvakuśala.

questions: Munidatta calls the poet Kṛṣṇācārya. I kept that form in the translations, marked [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}. Should the woven commentary use Kāṇha throughout instead?

cp.09.m3: I read bhagavatīnairātmāsaṅgatayā as 'through attachment to the Blessed Lady Nairātmā' (āsaṅga; the Tibetan has chags pa), not 'through union with' (saṅgata). If you accept this, the definitions of karini, mada and p-bhagavati, which say 'union', need the same change.

cp.09.m2, the verse attributed to Nāgārjuna: should line 1 stay as printed (jñānañ ca vīkṣya cyavat, 'knowledge, when examined, slips away'), or be emended to jñānañ ca bāhyārthavat, 'knowledge is like the external object'? The emendation is supported by the Tibetan and the metre.
cp.09.m5: can the edition settle whether damanaṃ or madanaṃ is the manuscript reading? The Tibetan (myos pa, 'intoxication') supports madanaṃ; I translated damanaṃ ('tame').

Draft line 1a has one 'post'. Munidatta has a pair of pillars (stambhadvaya), which he apparently identifies with the syllables e and vaṃ themselves, and the Tibetan song has ka gnyis, 'two pillars'. Should 1a read 'posts'?
cp.09.m3: I rendered īrṣyāmada 'the ichor of jealousy' (īrṣyā, 'jealousy'). The mada entry says 'ichor of passion'. Which do you prefer?

cp.09.m4: Munidatta names the source of the verse nāpaneyam ataḥ kiñcit… as a 'Madhyamakaśāstra'. The verse is well known from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra and the Ratnagotravibhāga (verse numbers from memory, to be checked). Should the tx-madhyamakasastra entry mention this?
